books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, C. A Temporary Truce on the Slavery Question in the Pre-Civil War Period

stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the House of Representatives’ gag rule, first adopted in 1836: Any petition or resolution about slavery would be laid on the table without being read, printed, or debated. The rule stayed in force until 1844. Former president John Quincy Adams, then a member of the House from Massachusetts, fought the rule in every session.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the House gag resolutions (Pinckney resolutions), 1836-1844, as described in Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.3 C, and Princeton Review 25e, Chapter 8, 'The Abolition Movement.'

source: original; stimulus paraphrases the House gag rule, 1836-1844, from the grounding books
stem: John Quincy Adams’s fight against the gag rule is most notable because he

options.text: wrote the gag rule himself and then opposed it in every session
options.misconception: Southern members wrote the rule; Adams spent eight years fighting it.

options.text: was the only Northerner who opposed slavery
options.misconception: Many Northerners opposed slavery; Adams was the most prominent fighter in the House, not the only opponent.

options.text: served as Speaker of the House during the fight
options.misconception: Adams served as an ordinary member of the House, not as Speaker.

options.text: was a former president in the House, using his standing to force debate

rationales.A: The gag resolutions came from Southern members. Adams opposed them from the start and fought them in every session until they fell.
rationales.B: Adams was not alone. Northern abolitionists and many Northern voters opposed slavery; Adams was the fight’s leader in the House, not its only voice.
rationales.C: Adams held no leadership post in the House. He was a Massachusetts representative, and his weight came from having been president.
rationales.D: Adams is the only former president to serve in the House, and he used that standing to force slavery petitions onto the floor again and again, until the rule was repealed in 1844.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who Adams was in the 1830s. A former president, now a representative from Massachusetts.
2. Ask what he did. He fought the gag rule in every session, forcing the House to face the petitions.
3. Ask why that matters. A former president arguing to be heard carries weight no ordinary member has.
4. Put it together. The notable thing is the standing he brought, not an office he held.
Background: Adams was elected to the House after his presidency and led the effort to bring antislavery resolutions to the floor.
Remember: a person’s past office can be the source’s whole point, so note it.
